notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes for Acts 22, drawn from the approved sources.

---

## Acts 22 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary

### v. 1 — “Brothers and fathers, listen now to my defense before you.”

Paul begins with the identical formula Stephen used in Acts 7:2: “Brethren and fathers.” The address is really two-fold — “brethren” for his countrymen and “fathers” for the elders and Sanhedrin members present. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/22.htm)

The word “defense” (Greek *apologia*) was a technical term in Greek law courts for a formal reply to an accusation. From it we get “apologetics.” It has nothing to do with saying “I’m sorry”; it refers to a reasoned argument presenting compelling proof. Paul’s defense here consisted entirely of his personal testimony. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-22-commentary)

Gill notes the remarkable grace of Paul in calling this mob “brethren” and “fathers” when they had just dragged him from the temple and beaten him mercilessly — and scarcely deserved the name “men.” (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/acts/22.htm)

### v. 2 — “When they heard him speak to them in Hebrew, they became even more silent.”

The “Hebrew tongue” is almost certainly Aramaic, the common spoken language of Palestinian Jews. The crowd had already hushed when Paul gestured for silence (Acts 21:40), but when they heard their mother tongue, they became “even more quiet.” Ellicott says the opening words did the work they were meant to do — one who spoke in Hebrew was not likely to blaspheme the sacred Hebrew books, so they were conciliated. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/22.htm)

Guzik notes: the Roman commander (Claudius Lysias) would not have fully understood the Aramaic speech, which is why he later resorts to scourging to find out what Paul said. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-22/)

Precept Austin emphasises this as a model for personal witness — Paul found common ground before sharing his testimony. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-22-commentary)

### v. 3 — “I am a Jew, born in Tarsus of Cilicia, but raised in this city. I was educated at the feet of Gamaliel…”

Paul counters the charge of being anti-Jewish by asserting his pure Jewish pedigree. “I am indeed a Jew” — the Greek places “a Jew” emphatically first. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-22-commentary)

“Brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel”: Ellicott explains that rabbis sat on a raised chair while scholars sat on the ground, hence literally “at the feet.” Paul’s education likely began around age twelve, when a Jewish boy became a “son of the Law.” Gamaliel was the most prestigious rabbi of the day (see Acts 5:34). (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/22.htm)

“Strict conformity to the law of our fathers” — Paul uses a word meaning “accuracy” or “exactness.” He had been trained in the most rigorous Pharisaic tradition. Ellicott notes a subtle distinction: Paul says he was “zealous for God,” while the crowd were “zealous for the Law” — Paul’s zeal had a higher object. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/22.htm)

Guzik observes: “It’s as if Paul searched for the nicest thing he could say about a mob that had just tried to murder him. ‘Well, I can say that you are zealous toward God.’” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-22/)

### v. 4 — “I persecuted this Way even to the death, detaining both men and women and throwing them into prison.”

“This Way” is the colloquial term early Christians used for their movement (see Acts 9:2; 19:9, 23). Ellicott says it indicated that they had found in Christ “the way of eternal life,” though outsiders may have used it with a tone of scorn. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/22.htm)

“Unto the death” — Paul was responsible for the deaths of some Christians (cf. Acts 26:10-11). Guzik notes the force of Paul’s implicit statement to the mob: “You tried to kill me, but I succeeded in killing many.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-22/)

“Both men and women” — Paul was unsparing; he persecuted indiscriminately. The Pulpit Commentary cross-references Acts 8:3 and 9:2. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/acts/22.htm)

### v. 5 — “As the high priest and the whole Council can testify about me… I obtained letters…”

Paul appeals to the very authorities who had sanctioned his persecution. Ellicott notes that Annas (with Caiaphas) was high priest at the time of Paul’s conversion, but now Ananias son of Nebedaeus held the office — yet the official acts of predecessors would be known to the current high priest. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/22.htm)

“All the estate of the elders” — likely the Sanhedrin or possibly the *Gerousia* (Senate), a permanent committee within it. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/22.htm)

“Letters unto the brethren” — interestingly, the Jews used the language of “brethren” among themselves, which the church later adopted. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/22.htm)

“To be punished” — Ellicott notes this could include imprisonment, scourging, brutal violence, or death by stoning (as with Stephen). (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/22.htm)

### v. 6 — “About noon as I was approaching Damascus, suddenly a bright light from heaven flashed around me.”

The note of the hour (“about noon”) is not given in the Acts 9 account and is a mark of Paul’s personal recollection. The light was brighter than the midday Middle Eastern sun. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/22.htm)

### v. 7 — “I fell to the ground and heard a voice say to me, ‘Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me?’”

The Hebrew form of Paul’s name, “Saul,” is used. The repetition “Saul, Saul” signals a divine address of urgency and compassion. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/22.htm)

### v. 8 — “‘Who are You, Lord?’ I asked. ‘I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting,’ He replied.”

Paul learned that in persecuting the church, he was persecuting the risen, glorified Christ Himself. Guzik comments: “He didn’t really know who he was persecuting until this.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-22/)

### v. 9 — “My companions saw the light, but they could not understand the voice of the One speaking to me.”

This has long been discussed alongside Acts 9:7, which says the companions “heard the voice.” Ellicott resolves the apparent tension: they heard a sound (like thunder, cf. John 12:29) but could not discern articulate words. The companions “heard” in the sense of perceiving noise, but did not “hear” in the sense of understanding speech directed to Paul. To see and hear the risen Christ intelligibly was a privilege granted to Paul alone. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/22.htm)

Grant’s Commentary concurs: “His companions saw the light and heard someone speaking to him but evidently did not understand what was said.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/acts-22.html)

### v. 10 — “‘What should I do, Lord?’ …‘Get up and go into Damascus. There you will be told all that you have been appointed to do.’”

Paul’s question signals immediate submission. Jesus does not give him the full picture at once but directs him to Damascus where further instruction will come through Ananias. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-22/)

### v. 11 — “Because the brilliance of the light had blinded me, my companions led me by the hand into Damascus.”

A further personal recollection: Acts 9:8 states only the fact of blindness; Paul himself connects it with its cause — “the glory of that light.” The mighty persecutor had to be humbly led by the hand. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/22.htm) Guzik: “In persecuting Jesus he was spiritually blind, and then he was also physically blind.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-22/)

### v. 12 — “A man named Ananias, a devout observer of the law who was highly regarded by all the Jews living there.”

In Acts 9:10 Ananias is simply “a disciple.” Here Paul stresses his Jewish credentials — devout according to the Law, with a good reputation among the Jews — to show that the one who received him into the Christian community was no renegade but a respected, observant Jew. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/22.htm) Paul omits Ananias’s own vision (Acts 9:10-16), confining his account to what he himself experienced. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/22.htm)

### v. 13 — “‘Brother Saul,’ he said, ‘receive your sight.’ And at that moment I could see him.”

The address “Brother Saul” signals immediate acceptance into the family of faith. The healing was instantaneous — “at that same hour.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-22/)

### v. 14 — “‘The God of our fathers has appointed you to know His will, and to see the Righteous One, and to hear His voice.’”

Ananias’s words are reported more fully here than in Acts 9. “The God of our fathers” echoes Stephen’s phrasing in Acts 7:32 — this is the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, not a new or foreign deity. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/22.htm)

“The Righteous One” (*ton dikaion*) is a messianic title used also by Stephen (Acts 7:52). Ellicott notes the verb translated “appointed” (*procheirisasthai*) is better rendered “fore-appointed” — God had chosen Paul before this moment. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/22.htm)

Guzik calls verse 14 “a wonderful capsule of the duty of every one before God: To know His will, to see the Just One (Jesus), and to hear the voice of His mouth (His word).” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-22/)

### v. 15 — “‘You will be His witness to everyone of what you have seen and heard.’”

This mission — to be Christ’s witness — is identical to the commission given to the Twelve (Acts 1:8) and virtually places the former persecutor on apostolic level. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/22.htm)

### v. 16 — “‘Get up, be baptized, and wash your sins away, calling on His name.’”

**This is the most theologically disputed verse in the chapter.** It is a key text in debates about baptismal regeneration — whether water baptism itself washes away sins, or whether it symbolises a cleansing already received by faith.

**The Baptist/Reformed/Evangelical (non-sacramental) reading:** Albert Barnes (Presbyterian) states: “It cannot be intended that the external rite of baptism was sufficient to make the soul pure, but that it was an ordinance divinely appointed as expressive of the washing away of sins.” The external rite “will avail nothing without the pardoning mercy of God.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/22-16.html)

John Calvin, on this verse, argues that God alone washes away sins by Christ’s blood; baptism is the “inferior instrument.” When Ananias says “wash away your sins by baptism,” he means “receive the sign so that you may know your sins are forgiven.” Paul’s sins were already forgiven before baptism (since he had believed and received the Spirit); baptism confirmed and sealed that grace. Calvin warns against the “Papist” error of tying grace to the outward sign. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/22-16.html)

Thomas Constable (Dallas Theological Seminary) explains that the Greek participle *epikalesamenos* (“calling on”) is an aorist participle meaning “having called on” — the calling on the Lord precedes and is distinct from the baptism. Water baptism symbolises the cleansing that faith has already received (see 1 Cor 6:11; 1 Pet 3:21). Paul experienced regeneration on the Damascus road; baptism followed. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/22-16.html)

Grant’s Commentary: Baptism was “a public washing away of those sins of which Saul had been guilty in publicly opposing the blessed name of the Lord Jesus… in the eyes of men he would wash away his sins by baptism, not in the eyes of God.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/acts-22.html)

**The Methodist/Wesleyan reading:** Adam Clarke says: “Let this washing of thy body represent to thee the washing away of thy sins: and know that this washing away of sin can be received only by invoking the name of the Lord.” Clarke holds baptism is a sign and seal but not itself the agent. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts-22-16.html)

John Wesley’s Explanatory Notes say baptism “to real penitents, is both a means and seal of pardon. Nor did God ordinarily in the primitive Church bestow this on any, unless through this.” Wesley thus sees baptism as the ordinary means through which God conveys pardon, while not strictly identifying the water with the washing. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/acts-22.html)

**The Anglican reading (Ellicott/Pulpit):** Ellicott says these words show that for Paul “baptism was no formal or ceremonial act, but was joined with repentance, and, faith being presupposed, brought with it the assurance of a real forgiveness.” He traces a line to Titus 3:5 (“washing of regeneration”). The Pulpit Commentary similarly links to 1 Cor 6:11 and Eph 5:26, seeing a close connection between the sacramental sign and renewing grace. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/22.htm)

**The Restoration Movement (Churches of Christ) reading:** Coffman insists the text means “Submit to the rite in order to be forgiven,” quoting Hackett approvingly. He rejects any notion that baptism is merely a token. “Nothing is more clearly taught in the New Testament than the fact of baptism being ‘unto the remission of sins.’” Similarly, *Contending for the Faith* states: “The urgent necessity for baptism is emphasized… until a person is baptized he will remain a sinner!” (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/22-16.html)

**The Pentecostal/Charismatic reading:** Enduring Word (David Guzik, Calvary Chapel / charismatic-influenced) simply notes that Ananias commanded Paul to “Arise and be baptized, and wash away your sins, calling on the name of the Lord” without making a doctrinal point about whether baptism itself washes away sin. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-22/)

### v. 17 — “Later, when I had returned to Jerusalem and was praying at the temple, I fell into a trance.”

This refers to Paul’s first post-conversion visit to Jerusalem (Acts 9:26; Galatians 1:17-18), about three years after his conversion. Paul stresses he was praying *in the temple* — evidence that he remained a devout worshipper at the Temple, not a blasphemer of it. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/22.htm)

“Trance” (*ekstasis*) — the same word used of Peter’s vision in Acts 10:10. Ellicott says it describes a state where ordinary consciousness is suspended and divine revelation is received. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/22.htm)

Guzik notes Paul never referred to this temple vision in his letters; he mentions it now only out of necessity. “Paul’s Christian life was founded on God’s truth, not spiritual experiences, and he didn’t even like to talk a lot about his spiritual experiences.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-22/)

### v. 18 — “‘Hurry! Leave Jerusalem quickly, because the people here will not accept your testimony about Me.’”

Jesus’s command was urgent — “Make haste.” This fits the first hurried visit after Paul’s conversion better than his later visit with Barnabas. The warning was likely a surprise to Paul, who probably thought himself the ideal messenger to his fellow Jews. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/22.htm; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-22/)

### vv. 19-20 — “Lord… they know very well that in one synagogue after another I imprisoned and beat those who believed in You…”

Paul’s gentle objection: “Lord, they will listen to me because they know my story. I was the arch-persecutor; my turnaround will be persuasive.” He mentions specifically his role at Stephen’s martyrdom — “consenting to his death” (the identical phrase used in Acts 8:1) and guarding the executioners’ garments. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/22.htm)

Ellicott notes Paul probably used the Aramaic word *Edh* for “witness/martyr,” the same root used for his own office in v.15, creating a poignant link. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/22.htm)

### v. 21 — “‘Go! I will send you far away to the Gentiles.’”

Jesus overruled Paul’s objection. It was not Paul’s idea to go to the Gentiles — this was God’s plan, not his. Paul makes this clear to explain to the crowd why he seemed so friendly to Gentiles: he was simply obeying Jesus. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-22/)

Ellicott observes the words convey a *promise* of mission rather than the actual sending itself — which would come later at Antioch (Acts 13:2). (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/22.htm)

### vv. 22-23 — “The crowd listened to Paul until he made this statement. Then they lifted up their voices and shouted, ‘Rid the earth of him! He is not fit to live!’”

**The single word that ignited the riot was “Gentiles.”** The mob had listened patiently to Paul’s entire testimony. They could tolerate talk about Jesus; what they could not bear was the implication that God’s salvation was offered freely to Gentiles on the same terms as to Jews — implying equality between Jew and Gentile. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-22/)

Guzik notes: “These Jews did not have a problem with Gentiles becoming Jews. But they were incredibly offended at the thought of Gentiles becoming Christians just as Jews became Christians, because it implied that Jews and Gentiles were equal.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-22/)

The cry “Away with such a fellow from the earth” echoes what was shouted about Jesus (Luke 23:18; John 19:15) and Stephen (Acts 7:57-58).

Ellicott suggests the “casting off their clothes” and “throwing dust into the air” were gestures of violent, uncontrolled Oriental passion, possibly preparing for stoning (as in Acts 7:58). The verb could mean “shaking their garments” as Paul himself had done in Acts 18:6 — a gesture of loathing and dissociation. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/22.htm)

### v. 24 — “The commander ordered that Paul be brought into the barracks. He directed that Paul be flogged and interrogated.”

The Roman commander (Claudius Lysias) had not understood Paul’s Aramaic speech and could make no sense of the sudden uproar. His reflexive solution was to scourge the truth out of Paul. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/22.htm)

Guzik emphasises the severity: this was not a normal Jewish flogging but the dreaded Roman *flagellum* — a scourge that could cripple or kill. “Men often died or were crippled for life after a scourging.” This was standard practice — but only upon non-citizens. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-22/)

From this point onward in Acts, Paul remains in Roman custody. Guzik: “As far as this book is concerned, this was the end of his time as a free man, though not the end of his witness or his usefulness to God.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-22/)

### v. 25 — “But as they stretched him out to strap him down, Paul said to the centurion standing there, ‘Is it lawful for you to flog a Roman citizen without a trial?’”

Ellicott argues the “thongs” refer to leather straps used to bind Paul, not the scourge itself: stripped to the waist, he was tied to a whipping-post as Christ had been. The Greek word for “thong” is always used for tying, not whipping, in the NT (Mark 1:7; Luke 3:16; John 1:27). (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/22.htm)

Paul’s objection had two grounds: (a) it was unlawful to scourge any Roman citizen, and (b) it was an aggravated offence to do so without trial, merely as a means of interrogation (as was done to slaves). Under the *Lex Porcia* and *Lex Julia*, Roman citizens were exempt from degrading punishments like scourging without due process. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/22.htm; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-22/)

### v. 26 — “On hearing this, the centurion went and reported it to the commander. ‘What are you going to do?’ he said. ‘This man is a Roman citizen.’”

The centurion’s alarm is immediate. The better manuscripts read simply, “What are you about to do?” The centurion knew the seriousness: even binding a citizen without trial was illegal, and they had already bound Paul (Acts 21:33). (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/22.htm)

### v. 27 — “The commander went to Paul and asked, ‘Tell me, are you a Roman citizen?’ ‘Yes,’ he answered.”

The pronoun is emphatic: “*You* — the Jew speaking both Greek and Aramaic — are *you* a Roman citizen?” The combination was so exceptional as to be almost unbelievable. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/22.htm)

Penalties for falsely claiming citizenship were severe — Epictetus speaks of death for such fraud — so the verbal claim was usually accepted at face value. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-22/)

### v. 28 — “‘I paid a high price for my citizenship,’ said the commander. ‘But I was born a citizen,’ Paul replied.”

The commander (probably a Greek by birth) had purchased citizenship under Claudius, likely through a bribe to one of the emperor’s influential freedmen (such as Narcissus). The name “Lysias” suggests Greek origin, and he had taken the *nomen* “Claudius” from the emperor. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts-22.htm)

Paul’s reply — “I was born a citizen” — is more emphatic in Greek: “I am one even from birth.” This means Paul’s father or grandfather had received citizenship, perhaps for valuable services to a Roman general or administrator in Asia Minor. The exact means is unknown. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts-22.htm)

Guzik: “Paul was an extremely rare individual. It was uncommon to find such an educated, intelligent, devout Jew who was also a Roman citizen. God would use this unique background to use Paul in a special way.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-22/)

Bruce (quoted by Guzik) suggests the commander’s remark implied sarcasm: citizenship must have “become cheap of late if such a sorry-looking figure as Paul could claim it.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-22/)

### v. 29 — “Then those who were about to interrogate Paul stepped back, and the commander himself was alarmed when he realized that he had put a Roman citizen in chains.”

“Those about to interrogate” — the Greek verb had acquired the secondary sense of “examining by torture” (like the medieval “putting to the question”). (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/22.htm)

The commander’s fear was specifically about having *bound* Paul. Ellicott notes a distinction: the chains fastened to the arms (Acts 21:33) were not considered incompatible with citizenship (Paul later refers to his “chains” in Eph 3:1; 4:1), but binding with leather thongs as a slave was quite another matter and a serious violation. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/22.htm)

### v. 30 — “The next day the commander, wanting to learn the real reason Paul was accused by the Jews, released him and ordered the chief priests and the whole Sanhedrin to assemble.”

Failing to extract information by torture (now forbidden because of Paul’s citizenship), the commander takes the alternative of getting a formal declaration from the Sanhedrin. So far, the Jewish leaders had taken no official action — the commander had heard only the clamour of the mob. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/22.htm)

“He released him from his bonds” — Paul was unbound for the hearing. Guzik observes: “Paul received what he probably thought of as a dramatic second chance.” Paul would now speak before the very Sanhedrin he had once been a member of (Acts 26:10 indicates Paul had a vote in that body). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-22/)

## Summary of Key Denominational Differences

| Verse | Issue | Views |
|-------|-------|-------|
| **v. 16** | Does baptism wash away sins? | **Baptist/Reformed/Evangelical**: Baptism *symbolises* cleansing already received by faith; the aorist participle “calling on” indicates faith precedes baptism. **Lutheran/Anglican/Methodist (Wesley)**: Baptism is the ordinary *means* through which God conveys pardon — a “means and seal,” though not automatic (*ex opere operato*). **Restoration Movement (Churches of Christ)**: Baptism is the act through which sins are actually washed away; without it one remains a sinner. **Roman Catholic/Orthodox**: Baptism effects regeneration and cleansing from sin (not directly sourced here, but the Catholic reading aligns with the “submit to the rite in order to be forgiven” understanding). |
| **v. 17** | Paul’s trance/vision | No major denominational divide. All traditions treat this as genuine divine revelation. Ellicott (Anglican) and Guzik (charismatic-leaning evangelical) agree it was an *ekstasis* like Peter’s in Acts 10. Guzik notes Paul did not build his life on such experiences. |
| **vv. 22-23** | The crowd’s reaction to “Gentiles” | All traditions agree the riot was triggered by Jewish exclusivism and outrage at the equality of Gentiles in the gospel. No significant inter-Protestant difference. |
